name: Input-Output Machines — Finding the Hidden Rearranging Rule
whatIsIt: An input-output machine question shows you a starting line of numbers (the Input) and then several 'Steps', each rearranging the line a little more, one move at a time. You're not told the rule — you have to discover it by comparing consecutive steps, then use that same rule to predict a step you weren't shown.
whyNeeded: This trains pattern-detection under a strict rule: exactly one clear change per step, applied consistently every time. It's the same skill used in following any multi-step procedure or algorithm correctly.
realLifeUses: Reasoning sections of banking and SSC exams
Following step-by-step instructions or recipes exactly
Understanding how sorting algorithms work, one comparison at a time
Spotting a consistent pattern from limited given examples

vocabulary.meaning: The original, unrearranged starting line of numbers.
One stage of the machine's output, after applying the rule exactly once more than the step before it.
The one consistent action the machine repeats each step (e.g. 'move the largest untouched number to the next empty front position').
Numbers that haven't been moved into their final position yet — the rule only picks from these.

story.title: The Sorting Machine
story.text: Aryan's mentor shows him: Input: 9 40 16 27. Step I: 40 9 16 27. 'What changed?' she asks. Aryan notices 40 jumped to the very front, and the rest — 9, 16, 27 — kept their original order. Step II: 40 27 9 16. 'Now what?' 27 jumped to the second spot, leaving 9 and 16 in their same relative order behind it. Aryan predicts the rule: each step, the largest number that hasn't moved yet jumps to the next open front position. He confidently predicts Step III: 40 27 16 9 — and checks it's exactly right.
story.extractedProblem: Input: 9 40 16 27. Step I: 40 9 16 27. Step II: 40 27 9 16. What is Step III?
story.answerInStory: Step III: 40 27 16 9 — each step, the largest untouched number moves to the next front position.

visual.caption: Watch how only ONE number moves position between each consecutive step — spotting that single change reveals the machine's rule.

teachingGallery.title: Compare consecutive steps, not input to final
teachingGallery.note: Always compare Step I to Step II (or Input to Step I) — never jump straight to comparing Input with a much later step, since several changes will have piled up by then and hide the actual one-move-per-step rule.

examples.caption: A different machine: each step, the SMALLEST untouched number moves to the next front position, building an ascending order from the left instead.

standardMethod.summary: Line up the Input and each given Step. Compare consecutive lines one pair at a time to spot exactly what single change happened. State the rule in words. Apply that same rule, one more time, to produce the next unseen step.
steps: Write the Input and every given Step, one per line, lined up in columns.
Compare Input to Step I: what single number moved, and to where?
Compare Step I to Step II: does the same kind of move happen again (same direction — largest or smallest untouched — moving to the next front or back position)?
State the rule clearly in one sentence once confirmed by at least two consecutive comparisons.
Apply the rule once more, carefully, to build the requested next step.

alternateMethods.name: Track the 'remaining' set
alternateMethods.whenToUse: Any input-output machine question, as a double-check.
steps: After each step, write down which numbers are already 'placed' (moved into their final position) and which are still 'remaining'.
The rule only ever picks from the remaining set — placed numbers never move again.
This prevents accidentally re-selecting a number that already moved.
alternateMethods.example: After Step II (40 27 9 16), placed = {40, 27}; remaining = {9, 16}, kept in their original relative order.

workedExamples.problem: Input: 9 40 16 27. Step I: 40 9 16 27. Step II: 40 27 9 16. Find Step III.
steps: Input to Step I: 40 jumped from position 2 to the front. Remaining numbers (9, 16, 27) kept their original relative order.
Step I to Step II: 27 jumped from the end to position 2. Remaining numbers (9, 16) kept their original relative order.
Rule confirmed: each step, the largest untouched number moves to the next front position; the rest keep their relative order.
Remaining after Step II: {9, 16}. The largest of these, 16, moves to position 3. The last number, 9, stays at the end.

workedExamples.problem: Input: 50 6 21 33. Step I: 6 50 21 33. Step II: 6 21 50 33. Find Step III.
steps: Input to Step I: 6 jumped from position 2 to the front. Remaining (50, 21, 33) kept their original relative order.
Step I to Step II: 21 jumped from position 3 to position 2. Remaining (50, 33) kept their original relative order.
Rule confirmed: each step, the SMALLEST untouched number moves to the next front position.
Remaining after Step II: {50, 33}. The smallest, 33, moves to position 3. The last number, 50, stays at the end.

trickPractice.trick: Compare consecutive steps to find what moved
trickPractice.intro: Look at neighboring lines only — Input→I, then I→II — to isolate exactly one clean move each time.

questions.q: Input: 3 18 7. Step I: 18 3 7. What single number moved, and to which position?
hintLadder: 18 was in position 2, now in position 1.

questions.q: In an input-output machine question, how many numbers typically move position in a single step?
hintLadder: Each step is one clean, consistent move.
Multiple moves per step would hide the rule.

questions.q: Once a number has moved into its position, can the rule pick it again in a later step?

options.label: No — only untouched/remaining numbers are picked

questions.answer: No — only untouched/remaining numbers are picked
hintLadder: Only the 'remaining' set is eligible each step.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming multiple numbers can shift position within a single step, instead of exactly one clean move per step.
commonMistakes.fix: A correctly-formed machine question always changes exactly one number's position per step. If your predicted step changes more than one, re-check the rule.

commonMistakes.mistake: Accidentally re-selecting a number that was already moved into place in an earlier step.
commonMistakes.fix: Keep a running list of which numbers are already 'placed' after each step — the rule only ever picks from what's left in the 'remaining' set.

commonMistakes.mistake: Comparing the Input directly to a later step (like Step III) to guess the rule, missing the smaller single-move pattern hidden in between.
commonMistakes.fix: Always compare NEIGHBORING lines (Input→Step I, Step I→Step II) to isolate one clean change at a time before jumping ahead.

teachBackPrompt: Teach a friend how to find the hidden rule in an input-output machine, using the 9/40/16/27 example where the largest untouched number moves to the front each step.

revisionCard.summary: Compare NEIGHBORING lines (Input to Step I, Step I to Step II) to spot exactly one clean move per step. State the rule in one sentence once confirmed twice. Keep track of which numbers are already 'placed' — the rule only ever picks from the 'remaining' set. Apply the same rule once more to build the next unseen step.

gameMission.title: The Jungle Sorting Machine
gameMission.brief: Watch the jungle machine rearrange numbers step by step and predict what it will do next!

realLifeProject: Write 4 numbers of your choice as an Input, then hand-simulate 'largest untouched moves to front' for 3 steps, checking each step follows the one-move rule.

rememberIt.hook: Compare neighbors, not the whole gap
rememberIt.unpack: Look at Input→Step I and Step I→Step II to isolate exactly one clean move at a time.

studentQuestions.q: What if I can't find any single clean move between two steps?
studentQuestions.a: Double-check you're comparing NEIGHBORING steps, not skipping one — comparing Input directly to Step II (skipping Step I) will show two changes at once and hide the real one-move-per-step rule.

studentQuestions.q: Do all input-output machines only move the largest or smallest number?
studentQuestions.a: Those are the two most common rules, but some machines use other patterns (like alternating largest-then-smallest, or moving numbers to the back instead of front) — always verify your guessed rule against at least two consecutive steps before trusting it.
